levels.title: The Beginning
levels.description: Find and read the administrator onboarding note in `/home/cadet` to retrieve your first verification flag.
levels.objective: Identify the onboarding note in your current working directory and inspect its contents.
levels.studentTask: Find and read the administrator onboarding note in `/home/cadet` to retrieve your first verification flag.
levels.goal: Identify the plaintext onboarding file in `/home/cadet` and print its contents.
levels.context: You have logged into a newly provisioned Linux workstation as `cadet`, where system administrators leave plaintext onboarding notes in the user home directory.
levels.successEvidence: Directory listing and file output in the terminal, followed by flag submission.
levels.howToWork: List the files in your current directory, print the contents of the readable note to the terminal, and submit the token below.
levels.systemContext:
You are a standard Linux shell (bash). 
      User: cadet
      CWD: /home/cadet
      
      File System:
      /home/cadet/
      ├── welcome.txt (Content: "Welcome! Flag: FLAG{linux_basics_mastered}")
      └── instructions.md
      
      If 'ls', list files. If 'cat welcome.txt', show content.
hints: How do you see what is in your current folder?
Once you see the file name, how do you read it?
levels.clo: CLO-1: Command-line interface navigation, file identification, and standard file viewing.
levels.expectedEvidence: Directory listing showing welcome.txt and cat output containing the flag token.
levels.expectedWarrant: In Linux, standard files in the current working directory are revealed by ls and their plain-text content is printed with cat.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming files must be clicked to open
Confusing directory path with file name

levels.title: Hidden Secrets
levels.description: Uncover the hidden configuration file in `/home/cadet` and read its contents to obtain the verification flag.
levels.objective: Discover the hidden configuration entry in `/home/cadet` and inspect its contents.
levels.studentTask: Uncover the hidden configuration file in `/home/cadet` and read its contents to obtain the verification flag.
levels.goal: Display hidden dotfiles in `/home/cadet` and read the hidden configuration file.
levels.context: Linux hides configuration files starting with a dot (`.`) from standard directory listings to prevent accidental modification and keep workspaces uncluttered.
levels.successEvidence: Directory listing showing dotfile entries and terminal output of the hidden file.
levels.howToWork: Check the local manual (`man` or `--help`) for your directory listing command to find the option that includes hidden entries, then read the revealed file.
levels.systemContext:
User: cadet
      CWD: /home/cadet
      
      File System:
      /home/cadet/
      ├── .secret_config (Content: "FLAG=FLAG{hidden_files_revealed}")
      ├── public.txt
hints: What kinds of entries might a default directory listing omit?
Consult the local manual page for your listing utility to see how hidden entries are controlled.
levels.clo: CLO-2: Linux filesystem dotfile conventions and command-line argument mechanics.
levels.expectedEvidence: Directory listing with -a flag showing .secret_config and its decoded flag.
levels.expectedWarrant: Files prefixed with a dot (.) are hidden from standard ls and require the -a / -la flag.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking hidden files require root privilege

approvedHintProgression.title: Conceptual Reminder

approvedHintProgression.title: Procedural Guidance
approvedHintProgression.text: Check the manual or help for `ls` options that display hidden entries.

approvedHintProgression.title: Bounded Example
approvedHintProgression.text: Inspect `man ls` for the option that does not ignore entries starting with `.`.

levels.title: Environment Variable
levels.description: Recover the verification flag stored inside your active shell session environment variables.
levels.objective: Inspect the current shell environment variables to locate the exported secret token.
levels.studentTask: Recover the verification flag stored inside your active shell session environment variables.
levels.goal: Inspect active process environment variables and identify the exported secret key.
levels.context: No secret file exists on disk for this task; instead, applications frequently pass configuration values and tokens through in-memory shell environment variables.
levels.successEvidence: Terminal output listing the exported environment variable and its verification token.
levels.howToWork: Run a shell command that prints active environment variables in your current session, locate the secret variable, and submit its flag value.
hints: Where does the shell store global variables?
Which built-in or standard commands display active environment variables?
levels.clo: CLO-3: Shell environment variables, session state inspection, and credential handling.
levels.expectedEvidence: Environment dump showing the SECRET_KEY variable and its assigned token value.
levels.expectedWarrant: Environment variables are held in process memory and can be inspected via env, printenv, or echo.
commonMisconceptions: Searching disk files when variables exist in memory

approvedHintProgression.title: Clarification
approvedHintProgression.text: Are you searching disk storage or process memory variables?

approvedHintProgression.title: Socratic Inquiry
approvedHintProgression.text: How can you view variables passed into your current shell process?

approvedHintProgression.title: Conceptual Reminder
approvedHintProgression.text: Environment variables are printed using commands related to the environment.

approvedHintProgression.title: Procedural Guidance
approvedHintProgression.text: Try running `env` or `printenv` to view active variables.

approvedHintProgression.title: Bounded Example
approvedHintProgression.text: You can query specific variables with `echo $VARIABLE_NAME`.

levels.title: Needle in a Haystack
levels.description: Isolate the single critical error entry inside the system log file to extract the verification flag.
levels.objective: Search the system log file to isolate the critical diagnostic record.
levels.studentTask: Isolate the single critical error entry inside the system log file (`var/log` or `/var/logs`) to extract the verification flag.
levels.goal: Filter the log file by severity keyword instead of reading every routine line manually.
levels.context: System logs accumulate thousands of routine status messages alongside rare failure events, requiring pattern-matching tools during incident triage.
levels.successEvidence: Filtered terminal output showing the matching critical log line and verification token.
levels.howToWork: Locate the log file and use a command-line text search utility to filter lines matching error or critical severity tags.
levels.systemContext:
User: cadet
      CWD: /home/cadet
      File System:
      /var/logs/server.log (Large file with random logs. Contains "CRITICAL: Flag FLAG{grep_is_powerful}")
      
      If user attempts to access /var/logs/server.log, allow it.
hints: You need a tool to search for patterns inside files.
Where are logs typically stored in Linux?
levels.clo: CLO-4: Pattern matching, regular expressions, and administrative log analysis with grep.
levels.expectedEvidence: grep output filtering /var/logs/server.log matching the word CRITICAL.
levels.expectedWarrant: grep filters input streams and files by regular expressions or substring tokens.
commonMisconceptions: Reading megabytes of log files line-by-line without filtering

approvedHintProgression.title: Bounded Example

levels.context: Internal administrative services are often bound exclusively to the loopback interface (`127.0.0.1` / `localhost`) so they can only be accessed locally from the host.

levels.howToWork: Inspect the network dump or issue a command-line HTTP request to `localhost:8080` and read the returned payload.

levels.title: Encoded Artifact
levels.description: Decode the ASCII-encoded file in `/home/cadet` back into readable plaintext to recover the verification flag.
levels.objective: Inspect the encoded artifact and decode its contents to plaintext.
levels.studentTask: Decode the ASCII-encoded file in `/home/cadet` back into readable plaintext to recover the verification flag.
levels.goal: Identify the encoding scheme from the file contents and reverse it using a standard CLI filter.
levels.context: Systems frequently encode binary or structured text into printable ASCII strings (such as Base64) for safe transmission; unlike encryption, encoding requires no secret key.
levels.successEvidence: Terminal output showing both the encoded string and its decoded plaintext token.
levels.howToWork: View the encoded file to recognize its format, check `man` or `--help` for the matching decoding utility option, and decode the file to standard output.
levels.systemContext:
User: cadet
      CWD: /home/cadet
      File System:
      /home/cadet/secret.b64 (Content: "RkxBR3twaXBlc19hbmRfZGVjb2Rpbmd9")
      
      If user runs 'cat secret.b64 | base64 -d' output "FLAG{pipes_and_decoding}".
      If user just cats it, show the encoded string.
hints: The file extension gives a hint about the encoding.
Consult the manual page for the encoding utility to see how to decode.
levels.clo: CLO-6: Standard streams, Unix pipes (|), and data transformation utilities.
levels.expectedEvidence: Decoded ASCII string output from base64 -d.
levels.expectedWarrant: Base64 encoded data can be redirected or piped into base64 -d to recover plaintext.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming base64 is an encryption cipher requiring a private key

approvedHintProgression.title: Procedural Guidance

approvedHintProgression.title: Bounded Example
approvedHintProgression.text: Example: `base64 <decode-option> <filename>`.

levels.title: Access Denied
levels.description: Audit your delegated administrative privileges and use authorized elevation to read the restricted verification flag.
levels.objective: Inspect file permissions and authorized privilege delegation to access the restricted artifact.
levels.studentTask: Audit your delegated administrative privileges and use authorized elevation to read the restricted verification flag.
levels.goal: Determine why normal file access is blocked and use authorized `sudo` delegation to read the protected artifact.
levels.context: Linux protects sensitive files via ownership and permission bits (`chmod`/`chown`) while granting scoped administrative capabilities through `sudoers` policy.
levels.successEvidence: Terminal output showing permission/sudo inspection and authorized retrieval of the protected token.
levels.howToWork: Inspect the file permissions and `sudo` policy in your workspace, consult `man sudo` for listing or invoking delegated privileges, and read the protected target.
constraints: Scoped sudo delegation enabled for user cadet
levels.systemContext:
User: cadet
      CWD: /home/cadet
      File System:
      /root/flag.txt (Content: "FLAG{sudo_power_unlocked}", Owner: root, Mode: 600)
      
      If 'cat /root/flag.txt' -> "Permission denied".
      If 'sudo cat /root/flag.txt' -> Show flag.
hints: What prefix allows you to run a command as the 'super user'?
Which option in `man sudo` lists your authorized commands?
levels.clo: CLO-7: POSIX permissions, discretionary access control, and superuser delegation (sudo).
levels.expectedEvidence: Output of sudo cat /root/flag.txt demonstrating permission override.
levels.expectedWarrant: Files restricted to root (0600) require sudo privileges to read.

approvedHintProgression.title: Clarification
approvedHintProgression.text: What error message did the operating system return when you accessed the target file?

approvedHintProgression.title: Socratic Inquiry
approvedHintProgression.text: Who owns the restricted file, and how can you check what elevated privileges your account has?

approvedHintProgression.title: Conceptual Reminder
approvedHintProgression.text: The `sudo` command executes programs with delegated administrative security privileges.

approvedHintProgression.title: Procedural Guidance
approvedHintProgression.text: Inspect your delegated privileges with `sudo -l` or prefix your inspection command with `sudo`.

approvedHintProgression.title: Bounded Example
approvedHintProgression.text: Example: `sudo <command> <restricted_path>`.

levels.title: Lost Data
levels.description: Search recursively through the multi-level directory tree to locate the misplaced backup file and read its verification flag.

levels.studentTask: Search recursively through the directory tree (`var/` or `/var`) to locate the misplaced backup file and read its verification flag.
levels.goal: Use a recursive filesystem traversal command to find the exact path of the misplaced artifact.
levels.context: When files are buried inside deep directory hierarchies, manual folder-by-folder navigation is impractical; operators use recursive search utilities to match files by name or metadata.
levels.successEvidence: Terminal output showing the discovered file path from a recursive search and its verification token.
levels.howToWork: Use a recursive directory search tool (`find`), check `man find` for filename or hidden-file matching options, and display the contents of the discovered file.
levels.systemContext:
User: cadet
      CWD: /home/cadet
      File System:
      /var/lib/misc/subdir/lost_flag.txt (Content: "FLAG{find_command_expert}")

      If 'cat [path]' -> show flag.
hints: There is a command specifically named for 'finding' things.
Consult `man find` to see how to match entries by name or type.
levels.clo: CLO-8: Hierarchical filesystem traversal and pattern-based search using find.
levels.expectedEvidence: find output returning /var/lib/misc/subdir/lost_flag.txt and cat output of that file.
levels.expectedWarrant: find recursively searches directories for filenames matching specified criteria.
